newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks money to improve U.S. economic data.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks money to improve U.S. economic data.

text.p: The White House on Thursday asked for money to improve the nation's economic statistics, saying their reputation has suffered as cash-strapped federal agencies have struggled to keep pace with a changing economy.

President Clinton's budget would, among other things, provide $17.5 million for improvements and revisions to the Consumer Price Index -- a proposal that follows criticism of the index by a prestigious panel of economists and by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
The agency that produces gross domestic product statistics would also get a boost in its funding.
The newly released budget plan said statistical agencies have made some progress toward improving the usefulness of the data, but more needs to be done.

"Rapid changes in our economy and society, coupled with limited resources to enable the statistical agencies to keep pace with these changes, have eroded the relevance and the reputation of the statistical system," the White House said.
Still, it added that many of the problems could be fixed through some specific initiatives.

Concerning the CPI, the Clinton budget seeks $2.1 million for the Labour Department's Bureau of Labour Statistics to launch a multi-year effort to look at ways to better capture quality improvements in goods and services measured by the index. The funding also covers a study of possible alternative measures for the cost of living.

Another $15.4 million would go for a continuing revision of the CPI that began two years ago and is scheduled to be finished in the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1, 2000. In all, the bureau seeks an $18.6 million increase in its budget to $379.4 million.
The issue of suspected flaws in the CPI has been a controversial one because the index is used to make cost-of-living adjustments to tax brackets and benefit programmes like Social Security.
A congressionally appointed commission, led by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin, has concluded that the CPI overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage points a year.

Saying the errors in the CPI were costing the government billions of dollars in overpayment of benefits, the Boskin panel recommended providing money to the Bureau of Labour Statistics for technical improvements to the CPI.
However, it said such technical changes alone may not be sufficient and suggested that Congress consider altering the way it indexes federal programmes to cost-of-living changes.
That advice was echoed by Fed Chairman Greenspan.
The Clinton administration has taken a cautious approach on the sensitive subject, saying any changes to the CPI should be "studied carefully and justified thoroughly."
